produced_by: Prompt 83 (dashboard data export). Pipeline walkthrough pulled from the ladder/closeout docs cited on each step -- not re-summarised from memory.

steps.description: StatsBomb open event data plus 360 freeze-frames (every visible player's position at each on-ball event) for the 2022 World Cup and Euro 2024: 115 matches.

Active defending = on-ball actions (pressures, tackles, interceptions, recoveries, blocks, clearances). Passive defending = where each off-ball defender is standing at each attacking on-ball event, from the 360 frames.
steps.source: train_active_binary_baseline.py / train_active_continuous_baseline.py (32 locked ACTIVE features); train_passive_continuous_baseline.py (38 locked PASSIVE features); train_passive_xt_baseline.py load_data docstring (1,593,181 rows, 198,354 events)

steps.description: Will a shot follow within 10 seconds (binary)? How dangerous is it, in xG (continuous, hurdle model)? How much expected threat (xT) changed (continuous, two-stage model)? Asked separately for the active and passive views.
23 whole matches are held out as a final test set and read once per model; the other 92 are split into 5 cross-validation folds by match, so no match ever leaks between training and testing.

Each leg starts from a simple baseline (Rung 0), then tries one change per rung: curvature terms, interactions, random forest, gradient boosting. A rung only replaces the standing model if a paired significance test on the 5 CV folds says the change is real -- and the rung's own motivating diagnostic actually moves.
steps.source: each leg's *_MODEL_LADDER.md section 1 ('What a rung is')

steps.description: Winning a rung is not enough to become the reference model. A 3-5 check audit follows: does it win in BOTH tournaments, does it regress on any error slice, do its feature shapes make football sense, and does the win survive the full end-to-end pipeline on the held-out test set?
steps.source: MODELLING_CLOSEOUT.md section 4; ACTIVE_XT_MODEL_LADDER.md section 5; PASSIVE_XT_MODEL_LADDER.md section 5

steps.description: All six reference models side by side, with an explicit rule not to rank binary and continuous legs on one axis.

honest_result_callouts.title: Gradient boosting won on error -- and still wasn't promoted
honest_result_callouts.summary: x1d_gradient_boosting beat the random forest on RMSE in a significant, 5-of-5-fold way (p=0.0031), but its rank correlation dropped (-0.0255 Spearman held-out) and the tail-calibration gap the random forest had closed widened back out 2-5x. The RMSE edge was about 1/17th the size of the random forest's own edge over the baseline. x1c_random_forest stayed.

honest_result_callouts.title: A slightly better score that wasn't statistically real
honest_result_callouts.summary: y1d_gradient_boosting nudged RMSE and R-squared in its favour, but the paired test was not significant (p=0.0635; Wilcoxon p=0.125) and held-out Spearman fell from 0.3154 to 0.2732 (~13%). An insignificant edge with a real ranking cost was not promoted; y1c_random_forest stayed.

honest_result_callouts.title: Significant, and still rejected: the bias got worse
honest_result_callouts.summary: y1b_quadratic beat the baseline in 5 of 5 folds (p=0.0006) -- but the one thing it existed to fix, a systematic over-prediction, got slightly worse (held-out bias +0.00278 -> +0.00298). Changing model family, not adding terms, was the fix: y1c_random_forest took the bias to -0.000018.

honest_result_callouts.title: Same lesson on the active side
honest_result_callouts.summary: x1b_quadratic was also significant (p=0.0018) with a negligible effect, and the tail-calibration gap it targeted did not narrow. The cause was the Huber loss capping extreme predictions, not a missing curve -- again fixed by the random-forest model-family change.

honest_result_callouts.title: Three independent attempts, zero improvement
honest_result_callouts.summary: The passive shot-danger model was never beaten: a curvature term (p=0.50), a full interaction expansion (skipped after it scored worse than the plain linear model on a real-data check, negative CV R-squared), and a random forest (directionally better on 4 of 5 folds, but p=0.576). Three different angles converging on 'no reliable signal to add' is reported as the finding.

numbers.d1c_interactions: skipped: CV R-squared -0.0249 / -0.0230 vs plain linear -0.0042

honest_result_callouts.title: Beating the baseline is not the bar -- beating the current best is
honest_result_callouts.summary: c1e_gradient_boosting significantly beat the linear baseline (p=0.0402) but tied the random forest (2 of 5 folds better, p=0.31) and sat between the two on every held-out accuracy metric. c1d_random_forest stayed.

honest_result_callouts.title: Better headline numbers, rejected on slice calibration
honest_result_callouts.summary: The uncalibrated gradient-boosting model had a strong overall calibration score but was 6-19x worse than its predecessor on specific phase-of-play slices. The calibrated version was promoted instead.

honest_result_callouts.title: Found while building this dashboard: a coordinate-frame bug upstream
honest_result_callouts.summary: Raw StatsBomb locations are in each acting team's own frame, but the data loader's direction-normalisation flips one possession team per half, so about half the rows in the locked feature files sit in the opposite frame from the rest. The rule-based phase-of-play labels inherit it (e.g. clearances labelled 'high press'). Every model was trained and tested on the same features, so the reported held-out metrics are real measurements -- but the spatial features are noisier than intended. Not fixed here (locked files); the dashboard's pitch coordinates are rebuilt from raw data so they are correct.
honest_result_callouts.source: dashboard_data/selection_and_frame_audit.json (frame_audit), produced by scripts/dashboard/audit_frames_and_profile_matches.py; explained in dashboard_data/README.md section 5
